items.title: International students, 'visa hoppers' and backpackers targeted in Australia migration crackdown
items.summary: The government wants to reduce net overseas migration to 225,000 people by 2028.
items.content:
International students, so-called "visa hoppers" and backpackers will be targeted under stricter rules announced by Australia on Thursday in a bid to curb immigration.

Foreign students will no longer be able to bring their families with them and those who want to extend their stay must choose a higher qualification.

Rules will also be stricter for working holiday visas - commonly used by backpackers and a crucial labour source for the agricultural sector - with a ballot system although these changes will not affect the UK.

The new rules were revealed by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke who said that while immigration was a "strength" of Australia, there needed to be a "high level of control".

For international student and graduate visas, Burke said: "We will no longer be adding to the stock of students automatically being able to bring family members over."

There would be exemptions for foreign students already in Australia as well as applicants from the Pacific and South East Asian countries, he said.

PhD students would also be able to bring their families as they were in different life circumstances to undergraduates, Burke said.

In a speech titled "The work of managing the migration program: who arrives, who stays, who leaves", Burke revealed a raft of changes as the government aims to bring net overseas migration to 225,000 people by 2028.

On student visas, he said the government would clamp down on "visa hopping" - where a student finishes a course, then applies to do another course which is often a lower qualification and sometimes with a "not so legitimate provider".

Students who want to go "up the scale" will be allowed, Burke said, for example, if a student finishes a bachelor's degree and then wants to complete a masters.

He also announced major changes to working holiday visas for those aged 18 to 30 years old who can work in Australia for 12 months, but can extend for a second and third year.

Currently, these visa holders must work for three months in regional Australia during their first year to qualify for a second year, and then six months to qualify for a third year.

Under the new changes, those who qualify for a second year will have to go into a ballot with a cap of 45,000, down from the 57,000 who qualified last year.

For the third year, the ballot will be limited to 5,000, down from 31,000 who qualified last year. British working holidaymakers will not be affected by these changes due to the UK's free trade agreement with Australia.

New figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday showed Australia's population grew 1.4% in the 12 months to March 2026 to 27.9m.

That total figure included births and deaths as well as a net overseas migration of 292,100.

Migration remains a major political issue as debate around Australia's population grows amid rising living costs, housing affordability and increased strain on public services.

One Nation, a populist right-wing party known for its anti-immigration stance and which has seen a surge in support in recent months, detailed its migration policy earlier this week, proposing to cut temporary migrant visas by 750,000 over three years.

The party, which won its first lower house seat in May , also wants to cap net overseas immigration to 130,000, drawing a rebuke from Burke who said such a proposal would risk "smashing parts of the Australian economy".

In July, the government introduced a policy to prioritise applications for family visas lodged onshore - where the applicant is in the country already - over those submitted overseas.

Skilled migrants already in Australia who applied for permanent visas were also prioritised over those applying from overseas.

It also paused applications for working holiday visas from 24 countries, not including the UK.

Violet Roumeliotis, from Settlement Services International which helps new arrivals to Australia, says the migration debate was increasingly driven by "short-term politics rather than what is best for the country".

"The proposed changes to family visas for international students is a good example of this," she said, adding that it would make it harder for Australia to compete for "future talent".

items.title: Rosenberg: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter
items.summary: There is no doubt over the outcome of this vote, but for the Kremlin they are still an important moment.
items.content:
The system of power in Russia is often referred to as "managed democracy" (where the Kremlin does the managing).

That means huge powers for the president and few political surprises.

This weekend's election is set to deliver another parliament dominated by the party of power, United Russia, and a house of MPs fiercely loyal to Vladimir Putin.

"We have our own political system, our own political process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained recently.

That means no curveballs for the Kremlin. No surprises. So no story?

For the Kremlin, the election of 450 deputies to the lower house of parliament, the Duma, is important. This is the first parliamentary election here since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Kremlin will use it to claim that most Russians back the president and the war, as well as to promote the political careers of soldiers back from Ukraine: officials say nearly two hundred war veterans are taking part in the election.

As for the election campaign, that has provided a window on Russian society four-and-a-half years into the war.

"Good evening and welcome to tonight's campaign speeches by candidates for Duma Electoral District 158," said the anchor on state TV.

The studio director cut to a wide shot revealing six empty lecterns.

"The candidates haven't turned up," admitted the host. "So, it's goodbye from me."

In another TV debate (where the politicians were present) one crooning candidate sang his pitch:

Yet a musical manifesto is strangely appropriate. In the previous Duma, everyone seemed to be singing from the same hymn sheet. At the final session of parliament in July, MPs stood and applauded as the speaker of the house chanted repeatedly:

It was a signal that all MPs in parliament should back President Putin and the war.

"All parties in the Duma, every single one, voted in favour of 170 laws to support the special military operation," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told me with obvious pride about the last parliament.

I caught up with Zyuganov on the campaign trail outside Moscow at a bread and biscuit factory. As I watched rows of identical-looking loaves speeding along the conveyer I thought about Russia's parliament. It's not that all parties in the Duma are identical: some are more nationalist, others – like Zyuganov's party - more left-wing.

But when it comes to backing the Kremlin's legislative initiatives and supporting the "special military operation" they vote the same way. Such "systemic" parties are vital cogs in Russia's Kremlin-centric political machine.

One such party - Yabloko - is calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. Back in July it was the only anti-war party in Russia to be registered for the election. Twelve days later, though, the Supreme Court removed it from the ballot. That was widely interpreted as a sign of Kremlin concern that anti-war messaging could strike a chord with Russian voters.

Despite Yabloko's exclusion from the party list, some of its candidates are still running in individual constituency races. Though in recent weeks growing numbers of Yabloko candidates have been detained by police, prosecuted for various offences and barred from the election.

"The police are carrying out a political order. That's no secret," Yabloko candidate Grigory Grishin tells me.

"This way, the authorities are setting the boundaries within which they believe the elections should take place.

"It is well known that the demand for an end to the bloodshed in this conflict with Ukraine is very popular. In my opinion, most people in Russia now want peace and Yabloko helped people express this. That's why it's been excluded from the party lists, and why individual candidates are being barred."

For now, Grigory remains a candidate. But the police recently came to his flat.

"Three policemen in civilian clothes asked me to accompany them to the station, which I did. The police said I had posted what they claimed was an extremist symbol: the word 'Navalny' and that, by doing so, I had propagandised extremism via my Telegram channel."

Alexei Navalny was Russia's most prominent opposition leader and Kremlin critic who died in prison in 2024. He'd been convicted on several charges, including extremism.

The Russian authorities insist that the Duma elections are transparent and fair. Critics of the vote point to opposition politicians who have been forced into exile or put in prison. Last year one of the leaders of a prominent independent election monitoring group in Russia was jailed for five years. Grigory Melkonyants was convicted on charges of working with an "undesirable organisation". His election monitoring group, Golos, has shut down.

Fifty miles from Moscow, in the town of Dmitrov, I see little sign of an election.

In the town centre there's a memorial to "Heroes of the special military operation": local people killed fighting in Ukraine.

"We feel it," says Olga, whose son-in-law is a soldier in the "special operation". "Because of the people who've gone to fight and the families left behind with sons, husbands, children and grandchildren there. But these elections can't influence what will happen."

"I'd like us to live in a peaceful country, with no war," Polina tells me, "So that you don't have to worry that a drone will fall down in front of you."

Russians have other concerns, too. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries have sparked widespread fuel shortages, while economic pressures are increasing.

"What worries me," says a barber called Ivan, "is that no matter how much you earn it's not enough. Prices are rising faster than wages. I speak to lots of people in my job. I know how hard-up they are."

"Western elections and elections in Russia are completely different things," Grishin explains. "Elections in the West are a way of forming a government, which is replaced later if voters aren't satisfied.

"Elections in Russia never bring a change in government. At best, they're a way of influencing it, of sending a signal. But power in Russia never changed because of an election. That's how Russia is."

items.title: Assad regime planned US journalist's kidnap for weeks, BBC finds
items.summary: Austin Tice’s abduction was approved by Syria’s former leader Bashar al-Assad, a source claims.
items.content:
US journalist Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria in 2012, was kidnapped in a calculated operation which was more than a month in the planning, the BBC can reveal.

A member of the group which detained Tice has also claimed the abduction was sanctioned by Syria's leader at the time, President Bashar al-Assad.

Tice was seen getting into a car with a driver he knew and trusted. For years, many assumed they had stumbled upon a government checkpoint, and that the abduction of the journalist had been opportunistic.

But we have uncovered evidence that, in fact, his disappearance was anything but chance.

In a new BBC podcast: Where is Austin Tice? Series 3 of I'm Not A Monster Presents , we reveal the findings of a years-long investigation into what happened to Tice, who had been reporting on Syria's civil war at the time.

His case has been followed closely by international media and cited by successive US presidents.

Josh Baker enters a dangerous world of fear, greed and betrayal as he uncovers what happened in one of the biggest missing-person cases of our time - the abduction of Austin Tice.

Georgetown University law student Tice, who had served as a US Marines captain, was last seen in a video - blindfolded and in apparent distress - posted more than a month after his capture.

As the regime fell 12 years later, tens of thousands of people emerged from the administration's prisons. Tice was not one of them.

We obtained co-ordinates from an intelligence source for multiple locations US authorities suspected he could have been held at, and searched for him for more than a month, but found no sign of him.

A former Syrian commander has said Tice was executed . Others have questioned this account and no remains have been found.

But in the aftermath of the regime's collapse, we did uncover secret Syrian intelligence files on Tice - hundreds of pages of internal records providing the first definitive proof that it was the regime that had held the journalist.

Two crucial questions remained unanswered, however: how exactly had Tice been taken in the first place? And, who was responsible for his abduction?

We have spoken to a number of men from the regime involved in Tice's detention, and have reviewed recordings of discussions about it. One man we spoke to, Abu Ali, is a former member of the National Defence Forces (NDF), a militia which was fiercely loyal to Assad.

He says the abduction operation began when Tice's driver - who multiple sources say had been passing the regime information for some time - told a senior NDF member that Tice was moving through rebel-held areas, reporting on the opposition.

Tice had pushed into areas most journalists deemed too dangerous and was writing front-page stories for the Washington Post. The Assad regime was cracking down on anyone highlighting its human rights abuses.

We have been told the NDF member Tice's driver spoke to was Sakr Rustom - not just any NDF militia contact, but nephew of Bassam al-Hassan, one of Assad's most trusted security figures and head of the NDF.

The information on Tice was passed up to Hassan, Abu Ali says, who is then said to have telephoned Assad.

Abu Ali says he was subsequently called into Hassan's office and told the president had approved the operation.

But Tice was not taken immediately. The driver, Abu Ali says, suggested that he and the NDF continue watching him, to uncover more about what he was doing.

Some time later, the driver reported back that Tice's actions seemed suspicious, Abu Ali says.

Tice, as a trained marine, would sometimes share his military experience with rebel fighters - according to several people we spoke to - and would correct fighters on how they used their weapons.

To the men watching him, that behaviour made Tice look less like a journalist and more like someone from the CIA. The BBC has found no evidence to suggest this was the case, and a former senior US official responsible for part of Tice's case has denied he was an intelligence officer.

In the days before Tice vanished, the driver made one particularly brazen move while Tice was interviewing rebel fighters. He secretly took the American's backpack, containing his MacBook, a satellite transmitter and other personal items, for regime operatives to look through, multiple sources say.

On 11 August 2012, Tice celebrated his 31st birthday at a rebel safehouse on the western edge of Damascus, a few miles from Assad's presidential palace. There was a swimming pool, Free Syrian Army fighters, Taylor Swift music and whiskey, Tice revealed in what would become his final tweet.

Then came the time for Tice to leave Syria. He had told various people he was planning to take time out in Lebanon.

But he was not heading to safety. He was heading to a state facility where Hassan had an office, in an area called Tahouneh on the outskirts of Damascus, according to several sources. Abu Ali was waiting there for Tice.

Abu Ali says Tice's driver told him that when he drew up to the gates, he pulled out a gun.

Tice laughed at first, Ali recalls the driver saying, apparently believing the man he trusted was joking. But the driver told Tice he was serious, Abu Ali says, and the journalist realised what was happening.

According to Ali, Tice pulled out his chequebook and pleaded with the driver to name his price, rather than go through with the kidnap.

NDF militia members then grabbed Tice, covering his eyes, Abu Ali says.

Another NDF member told us he would never forget Tice's expression as he realised he had been betrayed. Abu Ali says Hassan immediately called President Assad to tell him they had the American.

For years, the identity of Tice's driver has remained a mystery.

The BBC spoke to more than 20 people to discover who he was, with the trail eventually leading to the city of Homs, and the family of a man called Hamid Abu Obeid.

They confirmed he was the man who had driven Tice away, an account also supported by multiple NDF members. But by the time we identified him, Abu Obeid had disappeared.

His family say they do not know where he is, and fear for his safety. They say they were not aware of Hamid's involvement in Tice's case, and learned about it from him afterwards.

The Abu Obeid family, Palestinian refugees from Gaza, live in poverty. Under Syrian law they are not entitled to Syrian citizenship and live under significant restrictions.

According to Hamid's brother, he had been promised a passport, Syrian citizenship, a house, and a weapon, in return for delivering Tice - life-changing rewards. But after the abduction, the family says all he got was a pistol.

Then, after Assad's regime fell, Abu Obeid's wife says her husband was called by a man who knew about his involvement in Tice's case and was threatening to tell the US embassy, hoping it might help him secure asylum.

Abu Obeid urged him not to. He then took some money, told his wife he was going shopping, and she says she has not seen him since. She does not know if he is in hiding, or if he has been detained or killed.

Not long after he disappeared, she says masked men - some dressed in military clothes - visited and took a number of Abu Obeid's possessions, including his laptop and other devices.

The wishes of Abu Obeid's wife now chillingly mirror those of Tice's mother and family. On opposite sides of a disappearance that began more than a decade ago, both families are searching for the same thing: a loved one who vanished, and an answer to where he went.

items.title: US interest rates raised for first time in three years
items.summary: Rates were hiked in a unanimous decision despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for a cut.
items.content:
US interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years and could be increased further in a bid to slow rising prices.

Rates were hiked to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75% by the Federal Reserve in a unanimous decision, despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said the move was because "inflation is too high and has been for too long", adding that it was a "sober" and "responsible decision".

After the announcement, Trump expressed support for Warsh but said the Fed board, which votes on rate decisions, was "hostile".

Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for people wanting to secure loans, mortgages, and credit cards, but can lead to better returns on savings.

Warsh said during a press conference on Wednesday following the decision that, while there was "an attitude of optimism" within the Fed leadership, inflation remained a problem.

Like many central banks, the Fed has a target of keeping inflation at 2% or below. Warsh noted that US inflation has been above the target "for more than five years".

That has helped make affordability one of the top concerns of American voters, who have seen fuel prices surge in response to soaring wholesale oil prices since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran. This has driven up the cost of many goods and services, as well.

While the Fed "cannot affect any individual price – whether it be oil prices, whether it be food stuffs at the grocery store", Warsh said, the central bank can work to keep price rises from broadening across the economy.

He added that strength in the jobs market and wider economy meant the Fed was staying focused on stabilising prices, and that those least well off had the most to gain from lower inflation.

Central banks tend to increase rates when inflation is high to discourage spending and encourage saving, in the hope this will reduce the pace of price rises. But it's a balancing act, as higher rates can also encourage businesses to hold off on investing and hurt economic growth.

When he was confirmed, Democratic lawmakers had said Warsh would be Trump's "sock puppet" and many Fed watchers expected him to carry out Trump's persistent demands to slash rates. Trump had been heavily critical of Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell for not cutting them.

Asked on Wednesday about the message the rate hike sent to Trump, Warsh chuckled before saying: "I have got nothing for you on a discussion with the president."

Trump told reporters later "I'm relying on Kevin [Warsh], but he's got, you know, a very tough board".

"And the, interest rates are too high. They're not appropriate... I talked to Kevin and I said, 'you might as well vote with the board because it's not going to matter.' The board is very hostile, they're very political," he added.

Earlier, Trump said on social media: "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!"

Democrats on Capitol Hill said the rate increase would make loans costlier and, in turn, more Americans would go into debt.

"This is going to make everything become more expensive," said Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the Senate. "This is because Donald Trump does not know how to manage the economy."

The Fed's hike is the first rate move in any direction since they were cut in December 2025. The last time they were raised was in July 2023.

The increase could help push up mortgage rates for home buyers and lead to Americans paying more on other types of debt.

Major US banks JP Morgan, KeyCorp, and BNY all raised their prime lending rate on Wednesday to 7% from 6.75%, which will affect rates charged on credit cards and personal loans.

Mortgage costs have climbed over the past year but remain below peaks seen in 2023. A 30-year fixed deal is 6.76% on average, while a 15-year deal is 6.09%, according to figures from Freddie Mac.

Many US homeowners have 30-year and 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, and changes to interest rates will not impact their monthly repayments. But higher rates could affect those looking to secure a new mortgage or refinance.

Warsh declined to provide his own view on where he saw the Fed's rates going, but the majority of his fellow policymakers said they believe rates would be hiked again before the end of this year to between 4-4.25%.

A small majority also said rates could rise further to the 4.25-4.5% next year, before cuts begin in 2028 and 2029.

The forecast suggested price rises will ease in the coming years, with inflation, the measure used to assess the cost of living, predicted to fall steadily to the Fed's target by 2029.

The US Fed is not alone in facing rising inflation since the Iran war, with the European Central Bank raising rates last week and the Bank of England set to make its own decision on Thursday.

items.title: Snapchat open to putting time limits on teens, boss tells BBC
items.summary: Evan Spiegel says it would be "an important step forward for the industry" in an interview with the BBC.
items.content:
The boss of Snapchat-parent Snap Inc says the firm would be "willing to implement" time limits for teens, following a call from Meta for it to take action.

Evan Spiegel told the BBC in an interview at the company's California headquarters that setting a maximum amount of time that young users could spend on the app could be "an important step forward for the industry. "

His comments came as Snap revealed a slew of new features for its upcoming Specs glasses, which it said could connect to Apple iPhone and Mac devices.

Meta has been pressuring other social media companies to join it in making platform changes it agreed to as part of a recent multi-billion dollar legal settlement with US states.

Instagram and Facebook-parent Meta was facing allegations from Attorneys General for most US states who said the firm deliberately designed its apps to be addictive to young users.

It agreed to pay $12.7bn and implement a two-hour daily limit for teen users across its platforms by default, in addition to muted notifications during school hours, blocks at night and other measures.

"I think it is an important step forward in the industry in terms of really identifying industry norms, and I think that would be beneficial overall," Spiegel told the BBC. "We've looked really thoughtfully at the terms."

As part of Meta's August settlement , the company said it would implement even more stringent time limits and pay an additional $5.3bn if YouTube and TikTok follow suit. It has denied any wrongdoing as part of the deal, which will be paid over a 10-year period.

Last month, a Meta spokesperson said it was hopeful that Snap would make similar platform changes as well.

Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap have all faced a barrage of litigation alleging their apps have helped spawn a youth mental health crisis. Snap has also been accused of facilitating illegal drug sales.

When asked about the idea of a default time limit, Spiegel said: "I think that's a really good example of something that that we'd be willing to implement."

But Spiegel did not commit to a timeline on when Snap might take action.

"That's something we've talked about internally," he said. "I don't have more to share today."

He noted that Snap offers tools through its Family Center feature, which currently enables parents to track aspects of how their teens are using Snapchat.

"We want to figure out how we can be part of the solution," Spiegel added.

YouTube-parent Google said it had no comment when asked if it planned to implement the measures in Meta's settlement. TikTok did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Spiegel was talking to the BBC as Snapchat's parent Snap Inc announced new features for its upcoming Specs glasses.

He said the smart eyewear would use AI to suggest things for people to do based on what the tech learns about their goals, relationships and routines.

"Rather than the way that people use chatbots today where you constantly have to ask for stuff, Specs can understand what's important to you, and then offer recommendations or offer next steps," he said.

Like other smart glasses, Specs will use AI to let people see digital elements overlaid onto the world.

But the tech won't come cheap - retailing at $2,195 in the US and £1,995 in the UK.

"The target audience right now is early adopters of tech and developers as well as enterprise," Spiegel said.

With the device, Snap aims to offer a middle ground between VR headsets like Meta's Quest 3 and lightweight AI smart glasses offered by rivals which look more like conventional glasses.

"You have a really powerful computer that brings a lot of the immersive capability you see with VR, but they're also lightweight at just about 130 grams, so they're very wearable and they have these see-through lenses, so you can use them out in the world."

Specs is Snap's most recent foray into the wearable tech, coming a decade after its short-lived Spectacles cost the company tens of millions of dollars.

The device is also arriving as Meta is facing a significant backlash over its own smart glasses, which are estimated to be the most popular of the market.

Some online derisively call them " pervert glasses " over how they have been used to secretly film women, with one person telling the BBC they were filmed leaving the beach , while another said they were told to pay to remove a video of them from the internet.

Nevertheless, sales continue to rise. With seven million pairs having been sold according to Meta.

Snap said it has built into the design of Specs, which do not use facial recognition to identify people.

A white light flashes at the top of the glasses above the users nose when it is recording video and taking a photo.

The company says that will let people nearby see that recording is happening.

Users of Meta glasses have figured out ways to obscure components meant to indicate that a photo or video is being captured, including by tampering with the electronics in the device.

Meta says it has remotely disabled the cameras on thousands of its devices on which tampering or destruction of the indicator light was detected.

items.title: A Milano un rabbino ha denunciato di essere stato picchiato da tre uomini, poi individuati dalla polizia
items.content:
Un rabbino di 60 anni ha denunciato di essere stato aggredito da tre uomini mentre aspettava l’autobus alla fermata di Bande Nere, a Milano. L’aggressione è stata resa nota dal presidente della Comunità ebraica di Milano, Walker Meghnagi. Gli aggressori hanno un’età compresa tra i 19 e i 21 anni, e sono di origini marocchine e tunisine. Il rabbino non ha riportato ferite refertate in pronto soccorso.

Meghnagi ha detto che l’aggressione è avvenuta verso le 18. Secondo la sua ricostruzione, i tre uomini avrebbero spintonato e colpito il rabbino, e poi gli avrebbero tolto il cappello. «Hanno riconosciuto che era ebreo da come era vestito», ha aggiunto Meghnagi, che ha parlato di «aggressione a scopo razziale». Dopo l’aggressione il rabbino ha filmato i tre mentre si allontanavano verso la fermata della metropolitana e ha poi consegnato i video alla polizia, che è riuscita a individuarli. L’aggressione è stata commentata e condannata da politici di tutti gli schieramenti, tra cui la presidente del Consiglio Giorgia Meloni.

items.title: US House votes to hold billionaire Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt
items.summary: Black - who had business ties to Epstein - declined to appear and provide documents related to the convicted sex offender.
items.content:
The US House of Representatives has agreed to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for defying a legal summons related to its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Black, who had business ties to Epstein, did not comply with a subpoena ordering him to appear before the House Oversight Committee earlier this month and share documents related to Epstein.

Lawyers for Black, who has sued over the summons, called the contempt move "outrageous".

After passage of the measure holding Black in contempt, Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer said: "No-one is above the law. We will continue to seek transparency for the American people and justice for survivors."

In a statement shared with US media, lawyers for Black called the House move an "outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr Black".

"The full House is holding him in contempt without any regard to the active litigation challenging the lawfulness of the Committee's actions and the ethics complaint against Chairman Comer," they said.

The measure, which passed by unanimous consent, means the matter will be referred to the US justice department, which will decide whether to criminally prosecute Black.

In a written statement, the committee's top Democrat, congressman Robert Garcia, called the contempt vote "an important step towards justice and accountability".

"We will continue to center the survivors in our fight to hold those responsible for these horrific crimes," he said.

The private equity tycoon walked out of voluntary testimony before the House Oversight Committee in June after he was asked about nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) he may have signed, lawmakers said at the time.

Black left Apollo Global Management, which he co-founded, amid scrutiny in 2021 over his Epstein ties. He has denied any wrongdoing with regards to his dealings with Epstein.

The subpoenas, which ordered Black to share NDAs and give an on-camera deposition under oath, were issued after he left the committee meeting in June.

Black has said he hired Epstein as a wealth management adviser, telling lawmakers in June that he gave Epstein $158m (£118m) for legitimate reasons.

The billionaire has said he did not know about Epstein's crimes until he was charged with sex trafficking in July 2019.

items.title: Trump chief of staff Susie Wiles announces she's cancer-free
items.summary: The 69-year-old White House chief of staff is a powerful figure and particularly close to the US president.
items.content:
White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has announced she is free of cancer, exactly six months after she announced her diagnosis.

In a post on X, Wiles said her pathology tests "came back clear" after a visit to the Mayo Clinic earlier this week.

Wiles, 69, is considered among the most powerful figures in the Trump administration and someone particularly close to the US president.

In her post, Wiles thanked Trump for his "unwavering support" and vowed to continue working to "advance his America First Agenda".

Wiles continued working virtually at the White House during the six months of treatment following her diagnosis.

In a March statement, Wiles said that one in eight women are diagnosed with breast cancer.

"Every day, these women continue to raise their families, go to work and serve their communities with strength and determination," she said. "I now join their ranks."

Her post on Wednesday did not reveal any more details about her treatment.

Wiles is the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff - widely considered to be the most important role in the White House.

In her position, Wiles works to keep the president's agenda on track and serves as a gatekeeper to President Trump, as well as a policy coordinator and political advisor.

Before taking the job, Wiles played a significant role in President Trump's 2024 presidential campaign.

In December, Vanity Fair published interviews with Wiles in which she gave a blunt - and occasionally unflattering - assessment of her time working in the Trump White House.

For example, she described the famously teetotaling president as having an "alcoholic's personality" but added that there's "nothing he can't do. Nothing, zero, nothing."

She also provided candid thoughts about other figures close to the US president, describing Vice-President JD Vance as a "conspiracy theorist" and Elon Musk as an "odd, odd duck."

The US president, however, swiftly came to her defence and Wiles described Vanity Fair's reporting as having omitted "significant context" to create a "chaotic and negative narrative" about the administration.

President Trump and the White House have yet to comment on Wiles' announcement.

items.title: Canon EOS R8 Mark II, mirrorless full frame da viaggio. Piccola, stabilizzata e capace di scattare in 3D
items.summary: Tre anni dopo la EOS R8, Canon aggiorna la sua full frame più leggera con lo stabilizzatore integrato da 7,5 stop, un autofocus intelligente, il joystick posteriore che mancava e un linguaggio estetico completamente nuovo. L'abbiamo vista e toccata. ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Canon ha presentato EOS R8 Mark II, fotocamera mirrorless full frame, erede della R8 del 2023. Si tratta di una full frame leggera e "da viaggio", come l'ha definita Canon, all'intero della gamma EOS R.

Il nuovo progetto nasce, secondo quanto ci hanno raccontato, dall'ascolto delle esigenze espresse dagli utenti e ruota attorno a tre elementi: la stabilizzazione integrata nel corpo, che sulla prima R8 mancava del tutto; un corredo di funzioni ereditate dai modelli superiori, dal riconoscimento dei soggetti alla registrazione dei volti prioritari; e un design che rompe con la continuità estetica della linea EOS.

La fotocamera è inoltre la prima al mondo a integrare Dual Pixel 3D, la tecnologia annunciata oggi da Canon, che ricava informazioni di profondità da un singolo scatto e le trasforma in immagini stereoscopiche o in veri e propri modelli tridimensionali basandosi sull'analisi di parallasse di quanto catturato da due pixel adiacenti.

Il prezzo del solo corpo della EOS R8 Mark II è di 1.899 euro e la disponibilità è attesa per la fine di ottobre. È una cifra che merita attenzione, perché colloca la piccola full frame di Canon esattamente molto vicino a dove ora si trova, nelle promozioni, la ben più muscolare (ma meno nuova) R6 Mark II.

Il sensore è un CMOS full frame da 24,2 megapixel effettivi (25,6 totali), abbinato al processore DIGIC X. È lo stesso della R8 di prima generazione e della R6 Mark II: a cambiare non è il silicio, ma l'elaborazione che ci lavora sopra, a partire dall'autofocus, drasticamente rinnovato in questa release. La sensibilità nativa va da ISO 100 a ISO 102.400, estendibile a L:50 e H:204.800; in video la scala è ISO 100-25.600 con estensione a 102.400.

La novità strutturale più importante è lo stabilizzatore integrato nel corpo macchina, la cui mancanza era uno dei punti dolenti più sentiti del modello precedente. Il contributo dello stabilizzatore in-body è dichiarato fino a 7,5 stop al centro e 7,0 stop in periferia (secondo lo standard CIPA 2024, misurato con l'RF 24-105mm F2.8 L IS USM Z a 105 mm). Il sistema lavora in modo coordinato con la stabilizzazione ottica degli obiettivi, e in video si affianca allo stabilizzatore digitale di immagine. Come dicevamo, sulla R8 di prima generazione non c'era alcuna stabilizzazione sul sensore: è la differenza più pesante fra le due generazioni, ed è anche la ragione per cui il corpo è cresciuto.

Le dimensioni passano infatti da 132,5 × 86,1 × 70,0 mm a 131,4 × 90,0 × 79,7 mm: la fotocamera è leggermente più stretta, quasi 4 mm più alta e soprattutto quasi un centimetro più profonda. Il peso sale da 414 a 499 grammi per il solo corpo, da 461 a 546 grammi con scheda e batteria. Canon indica come principale materiale costruttivo la lega di magnesio, con parti in lega di alluminio e in policarbonato caricato a fibra di vetro, e dichiara una costruzione resistente a polvere e umidità, precisando in nota che la tenuta è garantita solo con il copriattacco montato sulla slitta multifunzione.

Sul retro, vicino all'oculare, compare finalmente il multi-controller, cioè il joystick per lo spostamento del punto di messa a fuoco, che era una delle assenze più discusse della R8. Mirino e monitor restano invece quelli della generazione precedente: EVF OLED da 0,39 pollici con 2,36 milioni di punti, ingrandimento 0,70x e refresh fino a 120 fps, monitor Clear View LCD II da 3 pollici e 1,62 milioni di punti, touch capacitivo.

L'ergonomia, ha spiegato Canon in presentazione, è stata riprogettata attorno a un obiettivo dichiarato: usare la fotocamera con una sola mano. Da qui la scelta più visibile, cioè la fusione dei due comandi che sulla R8 erano separati, l'interruttore di accensione e il selettore foto/video, in un unico comando sulla destra, che accende, spegne e commuta la modalità video senza spostare la presa.

Da qui anche l'impugnatura più larga, con una texture disegnata specificamente per questo modello, e la disposizione dei tasti pensata perché il pollice raggiunga il multi-controller e i comandi principali senza riposizionare la mano. Sulla ghiera delle modalità compare la posizione dedicata allo Slow & Fast.

Merita una citazione anche la separazione fra il vano della batteria e lo slot della scheda, che sulla R8 condividevano lo stesso sportello ed era una delle critiche ricorrenti: qui sono divisi, e con l'impugnatura EG-E2 montata si accede alla batteria direttamente dall'impugnatura, senza smontarla da treppiede.

Abbiamo avuto modo, a margine della presentazione, di impugnare la macchina, che pur risultando piccola (e questo è uno dei vantaggi), offre un grip assolutamente saldo, senza nessuna possibilità di instabilità. Il fatto che con la nostra mano il mignolo fosse "libero" non guasta, anzi permette di sostenere il corpo macchina da sotto. Chi volesse un'impugnatura più da reflex può sempre ricorrere al piccolo grip aggiuntivo, che però non aggiunge capacità di batteria.

La prima cosa che si nota, vedendo la macchina dal vivo, non è un aggiunta ma una sottrazione. Spariscono le "spalle" spioventi che hanno caratterizzato tutte le fotocamere Canon degli ultimi anni, e al loro posto arrivano linee nette e diritte.

È un cambio di impostazione che onestamente ci è piaciuto, rende la macchina più leggera e meno "gommosa".

Questo approccio stilistico era certamente presente in un lontano passato Canon, ed è il motivo per cui qualcuno ha etichettato la R8 Mark II come una fotocamera dal sapore vintage. Sbagliando, però: quelle linee non sono una citazione nostalgica, sono di fatto la direzione che gli altri, Sony, Nikon, Panasonic (sulle full frame) e soprattutto Fujifilm, stanno percorrendo oramai da anni. Con la R8 Mark II, semplicemente, anche Canon si unisce allo stile lineare che ormai è quello corrente per le mirrorless.

Ed è una conseguenza logica, più che una scelta di gusto. Le linee extra-curve appartenevano ad alcune reflex del passato, dove servivano a raccordare il corpo attorno al pentaprisma; venuto meno lo specchio, quel vincolo non c'è più, e la curva si è ritirata quasi esclusivamente nel grip, che resta l'unico punto in cui la mano impone ancora la sua forma alla macchina. E certo, la scelta di mantenere un richiamo al vecchio pentaprisma può richiamare forme del passato, ma con uno stile assolutamente attuale.

Il sistema di autofocus è il Dual Pixel CMOS AF II con rilevamento dei soggetti basato su deep learning: riconosce e insegue persone (occhi, volto, testa, corpo), animali (cani, gatti, uccelli e cavalli) e veicoli (auto da corsa e moto, aerei, treni), con copertura del 100% in orizzontale e in verticale, fino a 4368 posizioni di messa a fuoco e 1053 zone selezionabili. Canon dichiara inoltre una maggiore persistenza del tracciamento rspetto al passato anche quando il soggetto esce momentaneamente dall'inquadratura.

Il dato che colpisce è il limite dichiarato di luminosità entro cui l'autofocus continua a lavorare, che scende a EV -7,5: è la scena più buia in cui il sistema riesce ancora ad agganciare il soggetto, un livello di luce inferiore a quello di una notte di luna piena. Canon dichiara che il valore eguaglia quello dell'ammiraglia EOS R1; sulla R8, come sulla R6 Mark II, il limite era EV -6,5, cioè uno stop più in alto.

Va però letto per quello che è. Come tutti i costruttori, Canon misura quel numero nelle condizioni più favorevoli: obiettivo f/1.2, punto AF centrale, One-Shot AF, ISO 100. Poiché la messa a fuoco avviene a tutta apertura, ogni stop di luminosità in meno dell'obiettivo alza di altrettanto la base delle prestazioni: con un'ottica 24-105mm F4-7.1 IS STM, cioè proprio il tipo di zoom da viaggio a cui questa fotocamera è destinata in kit, si perdono fra i tre stop e mezzo e i cinque, e il limite reale si sposta in una zona ben più convenzionale.

La bella novità, già vista su macchine di altri produttori, è la possibilità di memorizzare fino a 10 volti nella fotocamera e fino a 100 sulla scheda di memoria, assegnando una priorità di messa a fuoco alle persone "catalogate".

Sulla raffica i numeri di targa non cambiano rispetto al passato: 40 fps con otturatore elettronico e 6 fps con prima tendina elettronica. Ma cambia la sostanza, perché cresce il buffer: con otturatore elettronico la R8 Mark II mantiene la velocità per 190 JPEG e 73 file RAW, contro i 120 JPEG e 56 RAW della R8. Con la prima tendina elettronica si superano i mille scatti.

Arriva infine il pre-scatto continuo in modalità H+, che registra circa mezzo secondo prima della pressione completa del pulsante e conserva fino a 20 fotogrammi precedenti allo scatto. Sulla R8 una funzione analoga esisteva solo nella modalità RAW Burst; qui è integrata nella raffica normale, con file ordinari. È una funzione che Canon ha introdotto sui modelli superiori e che, come l'azienda ha confermato in presentazione, non era presente né sulla R8 né sulla R6 Mark II con cui questa macchina compete.

Una precisazione utile, perché se ne era parlato nei rumor della vigilia: l'otturatore non è del tutto elettronico ma è presente una seconda tendina meccanica. Infatti la scheda tecnica descrive un otturatore a controllo elettronico sul piano focale privo di prima tendina meccanica, esattamente come sulla R8, con tempi da 30 s a 1/4.000 in prima tendina elettronica e fino a 1/16.000 in elettronico puro (1/16.000 disponibile solo nei modi Fv, Tv e M). Di conseguenza il sincro flash resta a 1/200 di secondo, o 1/250 con la funzione di priorità alla velocità di sincronizzazione su Speedlite compatibili, e solo con prima tendina elettronica: sale a 1/250 e 1/320 in ritaglio 1.6x.

items.title: Photos show widespread damage at US sites from Iranian attacks
items.summary: A wrecked air force plane and destroyed buildings are among the images obtained by the BBC's partner CBS News.
items.content:
Images showing widespread damage to multiple US sites in the Middle East from Iranian strikes have been obtained by the BBC's US partner CBS.

The photos, provided by active military personnel, show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings.

The undated photos were taken at US bases and sites in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.

One member of the military, who was not named by CBS, said: "This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public.

"We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face."

The White House referred the BBC to US Central Command. Centcom did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The photos, which have not been independently verified by the BBC, were published the day after a report from the Pentagon's watchdog confirmed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in the Middle East have been damaged and destroyed by Iran.

One of the photos showed a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Saudi Arabia that has been ripped in half, its tail section crumpled into a tangled mess of metal.

While the photo is undated, BBC Verify previously confirmed a similar photo , apparently of the same radar aircraft in March.

The Boeing E-3 Awacs are used to detect and track potential targets at long ranges to provide an early warning of possible threats.

At the time, a US official told Reuters that 12 US personnel had been wounded, two of them seriously, in an Iranian attack on the air base.

A pair of undated images reportedly from Camp Beuhring, Kuwait, show crumpled trailers, and a large tent-like structure that had been reduced to shreds as smoke billowed from the site.

Another image shows a four-storey building damaged by an Iranian strike at Camp Arifjan, in Kuwait.

Damage to the site was reported in March , including on satellite communications hardware, though it is not clear whether this image is from the same attack.

Brian Katulis, a former national security official under both Democratic and Republican administrations, said that the damage visible in the images showed that "America had not adequately prepared its defences".

"And there is strong evidence that US adversaries like China and Russia may have helped Iran in targeting," added Katulis, now a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute. "The Trump administration has done nothing to address these vulnerabilities."

The images were published on the heels of a report from the Pentagon's watchdog, which found Iranian strikes had "damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict".

It also noted that equipment losses have totalled $3.7bn (£2.8bn). Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (£24.7bn) on the war up to 29 June, the report said.

In the months after the war began, "dozens of US aircraft were destroyed or damaged", the report continues.

The document lists several of the aircraft damaged, including five refuelling aircraft which were "damaged or destroyed on the ground in Saudi Arabia by Iranian munitions".

A separate report , external from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) notes that the E-3 aircraft is no longer in production and would have to be replaced with a more modern equivalent, the E-7.

The CBO noted that the E-3 aircraft alone costs $500m (£371m), and the estimated total cost of equipment lost in battle - including planes, drones and a terminal high altitude area defence system - amounts to $1.9b (£1.4b).

CBO said that its review was subject to "uncertainty" because the defence department did not respond to its requests for information, requiring the agency to rely on government databases and public reports.

Additionally, the extent of repairs and rebuilding that the US military plans to do remains unclear, according to the report.

Brian Katulis of the Middle East Institute said that while "these costs show how the Trump administration burned through precious military resources without having much to show for it", the greater damage had been to broader US military readiness.

"The United States had to divert military assets from Asia to the Middle East, leaving America and its partners in Asia more exposed and vulnerable to China," he said.

"In addition, the depletion of US munitions makes Russia more willing to probe vulnerabilities with America's NATO allies and continue its aggressive war against Ukraine."

While the US has the financial resources to address the equipment losses, it is already facing budgetary problems and may not be able to do so fast enough to prepare for potential flare-ups in the Middle East or elsewhere in the world, he added.

Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country.

Since the war began Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel.

On Tuesday night, the US House of Representatives voted for the third time to end the war in Iran, approving a measure that would force President Donald Trump to end US military action without congressional approval.

The vote passed with the help of several Republicans, in what could be the final House vote on the matte r ahead of the US midterm elections in November.

It faces an uncertain path to passage - the US Senate has not indicated if it will take up the matter.

The same day, outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie announced an attempt to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth as new details emerged about the Iran war's price tag for the US.

The Trump administration backed Hegseth, with US attorney general Todd Blanche telling reporters he was "doing a phenomenal job".

items.title: Davide Fontana è stato condannato all’ergastolo per il femminicidio di Carol Maltesi nel terzo processo d’appello
items.content:
Mercoledì la Corte d’Assise d’appello di Milano ha condannato all’ergastolo Davide Fontana, l’uomo che nel 2022 confessò di aver ucciso Carol Maltesi, donna italo-olandese di 26 anni. La decisione è stata presa alla fine del terzo processo di appello, dopo due rinvii della Corte di Cassazione, che aveva ritenuto insufficienti le motivazioni contenute nella prima e nella seconda sentenza di appello (l’appello bis) relative all’aggravante della premeditazione. L’aggravante è stata riconosciuta anche in quest’ultimo processo (l’appello ter).

Il processo di primo grado si era svolto nel giugno del 2023 e si era concluso con una condanna a trent’anni di carcere per omicidio volontario, soppressione e occultamento di cadavere. Nel primo processo di appello , terminato nel febbraio del 2024, la Corte aveva invece riconosciuto le aggravanti della premeditazione e della crudeltà e aveva quindi condannato Fontana all’ergastolo.

La Corte di Cassazione aveva disposto un primo annullamento del processo di secondo grado, manifestando dubbi sulla sussistenza dell’aggravante della premeditazione. L’aggravante era stata confermata anche nella seconda sentenza di appello, che era stata nuovamente annullata dalla Cassazione per lo stesso motivo, dando luogo al terzo processo d’appello.

Del femminicidio di Maltesi si discusse molto sui giornali e in televisione, anche a causa della sua violenza: fu uccisa all’inizio di gennaio, ma i resti del suo corpo vennero trovati in un bosco solo a marzo, all’interno di alcuni sacchi neri. Fu riconosciuta grazie ai suoi tatuaggi, perché il suo volto era stato sfigurato. Durante un interrogatorio, Fontana confessò di averla uccisa, di aver conservato il suo corpo in un freezer per settimane e di aver continuato a rispondere al telefono della donna fingendosi lei.

items.title: Eight children among 21 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses, rescuers say
items.summary: Some 10 families had reportedly been living in the six-storey building in Gaza City that was hit by an Israeli strike last year.
items.content:
At least 21 people have been killed, including eight children, after a war-damaged building collapsed in the Gaza Strip overnight, rescuers and medics say.

Witnesses told the BBC that the six-storey building in Gaza City's Tal al-Hawa area had been left tilting dangerously to one side after an Israeli strike more than a year ago. Displaced families had lived inside because they were desperate, they said.

UN and Egyptian teams joined the search for survivors, which was slow due to a lack of equipment. Initially, rescuers from the Hamas-run Civil Defence agency had to use their bare hands.

On Wednesday afternoon, they said they had ended the operation after taking 45 injured people to hospitals.

Sherif, whose sister was killed, said: "They couldn't find a tent or somewhere to live.

"This was the last place they could turn to, despite the danger. They were aware that it would likely end in tragedy. A lack of resources drove them towards certain death."

A woman living in a tent nearby, Umm Mohammed Bakrun, said she had been talking to her son when the building collapsed suddenly in the early hours of Wednesday.

"It felt like an earthquake. There was a loud sound and I couldn't stand up. Stones rained down on us and when I looked outside I saw a lot of dust," she told the BBC. "Within minutes, there were screams everywhere."

Another witness, Mansour Abu Mohammed, said the building collapsed "in a few seconds".

"Every day, a stone or a few stones would fall from it, but the people inside couldn't find anywhere else to live. I used to live next door to it and you could see that it was tilting to one side."

Satellite imagery shows that the area around the building was targeted in the early weeks of the war, while damage to the building itself first became evident in 2024.

The head of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Gaza office, Alessandro Mrakic, told reporters at the scene on Wednesday morning that "the situation... is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed".

He also warned that approximately 400 other war-damaged buildings across Gaza were at imminent risk of collapse, particularly as winter approaches.

"We need support, most importantly with machinery, equipment, among others. Our colleagues here don't have [engine] oil and spare parts to continue to work with all the equipment that is still in Gaza."

The UN's humanitarian relief co-ordinator, Ramiz Alakbarov, said he was "devastated" by the reports of the building collapse.

"No-one should have to risk their life simply to find a safe place to shelter," he said.

He also urged Israeli authorities to approve deliveries to Gaza of heavy machinery for rescue operations, as well as tents, tarpaulins and other non-food items for displaced people ahead of the winter rains.

Israel says its restrictions are meant to keep equipment out of the hands of Palestinian armed groups that could also have military uses.

An estimated 80% of all structures in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged during the war between Israel and Hamas, according to the UN.

More than 1.9 million people - about 90% of the territory's population - have been displaced, many of them multiple times, and 1.2 million of them are currently living in tents or makeshift shelters, it says.

The UN has warned that the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire despite the ceasefire agreed last October, as Israeli air strikes and other attacks continue to hit populated areas, causing casualties and property damage and driving further displacement.

On Tuesday, Israeli air strikes killed at least five Palestinians, including two children and a Hamas commander, according to health officials and Hamas sources.

The Israeli military said it killed a Hamas commander in southern Gaza and another fighter in the north. In both cases, a child was also reportedly killed.

Separately, the British charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said that a patient was killed by an Israeli drone at a health centre it supports in Jabalia in northern Gaza. A spokesperson for the Israeli military told the BBC it was not aware of such an incident.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 73,790 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

items.title: Com’è che alcune città italiane vanno a prendere gli autisti di autobus in Tunisia
items.summary: Dopo Milano ora anche Brescia: c'entra il fatto che è un lavoro sempre meno attraente, ma anche i rapporti tra i due paesi
items.content:
Brescia Mobilità, la società del trasporto pubblico locale, ha assunto 28 lavoratori in Tunisia che a breve arriveranno in città e prenderanno servizio per diventare nei prossimi mesi autisti degli autobus. Non è la prima azienda di trasporti a farlo: nei mesi scorsi anche l’ATM di Milano aveva assunto una trentina di autisti sempre dalla Tunisia e sempre per far fronte alla cronica carenza di conducenti.

È un mestiere che in Italia per molte persone è poco attrattivo, per via degli stipendi bassi in rapporto al costo della vita, ma anche per ragioni legate al lavoro in sé. I primi lavoratori dalla Tunisia sono arrivati a Brescia mercoledì, gli altri arriveranno prossimamente così da avviare il percorso di inserimento intorno alla metà di ottobre. A Milano, secondo i piani, i nuovi autisti tunisini dovrebbero iniziare a guidare gli autobus dell’ATM da questo autunno.

I progetti di ATM e Brescia Mobilità sono stati gestiti separatamente, ma entrambi sono stati resi possibili da un accordo fra Italia e Tunisia che ha agevolato alcuni passaggi. È il Memorandum d’intesa di cooperazione in materia di gestione dei flussi migratori, sottoscritto a ottobre del 2023. Il protocollo attuativo di questo documento, firmato nel 2024, prevede una collaborazione tra Sviluppo Lavoro Italia, società controllata dal ministero del Lavoro, e ANETI, l’agenzia nazionale tunisina per il lavoro, per far entrare in Italia 12mila lavoratori tunisini in tre anni.

In pratica Sviluppo Lavoro Italia raccoglie le richieste delle imprese italiane e ANETI fa una prima selezione in Tunisia dei lavoratori richiesti. I lavoratori selezionati vengono poi inseriti in un percorso di formazione, che prevede corsi di italiano e apprendimento di competenze utili per il mestiere che svolgeranno poi in Italia. Il Memorandum prevede che i lavoratori tunisini possano ottenere il visto e il permesso di soggiorno con procedure accelerate.

L’articolo 8 del Memorandum prevede anche che i due paesi rafforzino la cooperazione per contrastare l’immigrazione irregolare. È un aspetto integrante e non secondario dell’accordo sugli ingressi dei lavoratori: in questi anni il governo italiano ha investito molto nel rapporto con il presidente tunisino Kaïs Saïed, facendosi per certi versi garante dell’affidabilità di un leader autocratico e illiberale, e convincendo l’Unione Europea a fornire prestiti al suo regime , da anni alle prese con una gravissima crisi economica e istituzionale. C’entra il fatto che nel 2023 è dalla Tunisia che era partita la stragrande maggioranza dei migranti che sbarcavano in Italia.

La Tunisia, comunque, non è l’unico paese con cui l’Italia ha fatto accordi per consentire l’ingresso di lavoratori stranieri già formati nel paese d’origine, al di fuori delle quote stabilite dal decreto Flussi , cioè la norma decisa dal governo che ogni anno determina quanti stranieri extracomunitari possono entrare regolarmente in Italia, calcolati sulla base delle esigenze del mercato. Ce ne sono altri , per vari settori.

Per quanto riguarda il progetto degli autisti degli autobus a Brescia, Marco Medeghini, dirigente della società del trasporto pubblico, dice che circa sei-sette anni fa l’azienda aveva già avviato una “academy”, cioè un programma di apprendistato, per cui aveva iniziato ad assumere a tempo determinato lavoratori da formare come autisti e a pagare il loro percorso per ottenere la patente D e le qualifiche necessarie. «Ma non è bastato a colmare le mancanze, perché continuano ad andare in pensione più persone di quelle che assumiamo», dice Medeghini. Per questa ragione l’azienda si è poi rivolta al ministero del Lavoro tramite ASSTRA, l’associazione che riunisce le società del trasporto pubblico locale.

Un autobus a Milano, 15 ottobre 2021 (ANSA/MOURAD BALTI TOUATI)

A Milano l’ATM è passata invece da Elis, un ente non profit, ma il percorso è stato simile . Una volta individuati i potenziali candidati, alcuni dipendenti di Brescia Mobilità sono andati in Tunisia per incontrarli e fare una prima verifica delle loro competenze sia professionali che linguistiche. Una volta in Italia dovranno frequentare un corso di italiano e altri di formazione, convertire le loro patenti (alcuni sono autisti di camion) e ottenere la carta di qualificazione del conducente (CQC), necessaria per svolgere la professione.

Per farli arrivare in Italia, Brescia Mobilità ha dovuto occuparsi preventivamente anche del loro alloggio. Tramite una convenzione con l’ALER (Azienda lombarda per l’edilizia residenziale) di Brescia, Cremona e Mantova ha finanziato con circa 500mila euro la ristrutturazione di alloggi popolari in alcuni quartieri della città (Casazza, Borgo Trento e Sanpolino), dove i nuovi autisti potranno andare a vivere in condivisione tra loro, pagando un canone d’affitto calmierato: 300 euro per una stanza singola e 200 euro per una doppia (con un aumento di 50 euro dopo 12 mesi, per un massimo di 24 mesi).

«È chiaro che si tratta di una soluzione provvisoria, perché così una persona non può portare la sua famiglia. Ma la nostra intenzione è avviare in questo modo un percorso più stabile», dice Medeghini. Oltre agli aspiranti autisti, Brescia Mobilità ha assunto altri undici lavoratori, sempre in Tunisia, come tecnici per la manutenzione della metropolitana cittadina. Medeghini dice che in futuro l’azienda punta a fare nuovi bandi per aiutare altri aspiranti autisti che potrebbero avere difficoltà con l’alloggio, a causa del costo crescente degli affitti.

I motivi per cui non si trovano gli autisti degli autobus in Italia, così come molte altre professioni, sono vari. Secondo Medeghini c’entra il fatto che è un lavoro che si svolge su turni; per i sindacati invece uno dei problemi maggiori è lo stipendio basso. Quello degli autisti degli autobus è regolato dal contratto collettivo nazionale Autoferrotranvieri-Internavigatori, che fissa lo stipendio medio mensile a circa 1.620 euro lordi per un autista neoassunto e a circa 1.900 euro lordi mensili per uno con anzianità lavorativa (considerando l’indennità di contingenza).

A questi va aggiunta l’eventuale quota del contratto integrativo aziendale. Medeghini dice che un autista di autobus a Brescia arriva a guadagnare 1.800 euro netti al mese. I nuovi autisti tunisini saranno assunti inizialmente come “autisti allievi”, con uno stipendio di circa 1.500 euro lordi.

I sindacati già un anno fa avevano detto che la quantità di ore che un lavoratore passa fuori di casa non è adeguata allo stipendio e che il mestiere è diventato molto più difficile negli ultimi anni perché il rischio di subire aggressioni fisiche e verbali è aumentato. Secondo Davide Bertolassi, sindacalista della FILT-CGIL di Brescia, c’è un altro problema: ci sono già altri dipendenti di Brescia Mobilità che sono in difficoltà per gli affitti, i cui prezzi medi sono molto aumentati in città negli ultimi anni, e per loro però non ci sono al momento iniziative di sostegno.

items.title: Il governo ha prorogato nuovamente lo sconto delle accise sul gasolio, ma lo ha ridotto
items.content:
Mercoledì pomeriggio con un decreto il governo ha prorogato nuovamente lo sconto sulle accise del gasolio, le imposte di importo fisso pagate su ogni litro di carburante. Lo sconto previsto dalla proroga diminuirà nel tempo: sarà di 12 centesimi dal 18 al 25 settembre, e poi diminuirà a 6 centesimi dal 25 settembre al 5 ottobre. In entrambi i casi è un importo minore di quello che viene scontato attualmente, pari a 17 centesimi, che scadrà il 17 settembre.

In seguito il prezzo sarà abbassato con il meccanismo delle accise mobili: significa che il governo si impegna a utilizzare il maggior gettito ottenuto dalla vendita in un certo periodo per abbassare le accise nel periodo successivo. Le accise saranno “mobili” perché la riduzione non sarà una cifra fissa, ma dipenderà dalle entrate legate all’IVA sui carburanti.

Contemporaneamente il governo ha annunciato anche la sospensione del bollo per le auto e le moto per il 2027: è una nuova misura legata al piano per contrastare il rincaro dei carburanti.

Per lo sconto sulle accise il governo ha speso dall’inizio della guerra in Medio Oriente quasi due miliardi e mezzo di euro. È una spesa enorme per lo Stato, e comporta anche un problema di equità: la riduzione delle accise si applica a tutti, in modo uguale, e non solo a chi ne ha più bisogno, quindi chi ha i redditi più bassi o ha maggiore necessità di usare l’auto. È inoltre una decisione che spinge ad aumentare i consumi – visto che una parte del costo è pagato dallo Stato e non dai consumatori – facendo aumentare la domanda, e quindi il prezzo finale. Dato che l’attuale situazione è caratterizzata da una riduzione dell’offerta, sarebbe più efficace limitare i consumi.

Nonostante questi problemi il governo ha deciso di rinnovare lo sconto, temendo che il mancato rinnovo sarebbe stato una decisione impopolare: in questi giorni infatti il prezzo del gasolio ha raggiunto il livello più alto da quando si registrano le serie storiche, dal 2005, e ha superato anche i massimi toccati nelle prime settimane di guerra in Ucraina.

items.title: Michelin-starred Seoul restaurant fined for using ants as garnish
items.summary: The owner of the acclaimed establishment avoids jail but is made to pay 15 million won (£8,144; $10,965).
items.content:
A two Michelin-starred restaurant in Seoul has been fined for using ants as a dessert garnish.

The owner of Evett in the South Korean capital was fined 15 million won (£8,144; $10,965), while the company operating the restaurant was fined 10 million won for violating the Food Sanitation Act, local media report.

Ants are not among the 10 insect species approved for human consumption in the east Asian nation. The approved list includes grasshoppers, locusts and some silkworms.

Prosecutors had sought a one-year prison term for the restaurant's owner, as well as a 20 million won fine - but the judge took the owner admitting the charge and having no prior criminal record into account.

However, the judge is reported as saying that, as well as violating food standards, the presence of heavy metals exceeding standards was detected in the ants when they were tested, meaning the "culpability is not light".

The owner was said to have been unaware that providing ants in food was prohibited in South Korea, as they are used as food elsewhere.

Their use as a topping for sorbets at Evett came to light after the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety found online reviews accompanied by photographs.

It said the owner had sprinkled three to five ants on certain dishes to give them a "sour taste", over a period of nearly four years - amounting to approximately 49,000 ants used as a garnish.

Most of the ants were imported from the US, while some came from Thailand, the ministry said.

The owner had argued that they were used in a "small part" of the restaurant's 15-course menu and that diners were told they could opt for a non-ant alternative topping.

Ants are eaten and sometimes even valued as a delicacy in several Asian, African and Latin American cultures. Weaver ants and their eggs are used in Thai and Cambodian cooking, while in Colombia, queen ants are as prized as caviar.

The Michelin Guide considers a two-star establishment as one that does "excellent cooking" and is "worth a detour".

items.title: Il governo ha sospeso il bollo per auto e moto
items.summary: Sospeso, non abolito: l’esenzione riguarderà le auto di piccola e media potenza e tutti i motocicli, per il 2027
items.content:
Il Consiglio dei ministri ha deciso la sospensione per il 2027 del bollo per auto e moto, un tributo che chi possiede un veicolo deve pagare ogni anno. Il prossimo anno non lo dovrà pagare chi ha un’automobile di piccola o media potenza (sotto gli 80 kW) e chi ha un motociclo: spetta però solo un’esenzione a persona, dunque chi possiede più veicoli non pagherà un bollo soltanto, quello con l’importo più basso. Il governo ha stimato che i veicoli coinvolti da questa decisione siano circa 14,5 milioni.

Il bollo è una tassa regionale, dunque il governo ha previsto una compensazione di 2,3 miliardi di euro da dare alle regioni per il mancato gettito. Al momento non è chiaro come finanzierà questa misura.

Nella conferenza stampa che ha seguito la riunione del Consiglio dei ministri, la presidente del Consiglio Giorgia Meloni ha detto che il governo ha «deciso di abolire in modo strutturale» il bollo, definito «una delle tasse più odiate dagli italiani». È una dichiarazione demagogica e fuorviante, perché la misura non prevede l’abolizione permanente del bollo, ma solo l’esenzione per un anno.

Fonti della presidenza del Consiglio hanno fatto sapere che è temporanea perché per ora è stata inserita in un decreto-legge, un provvedimento in teoria emergenziale , ma che il governo intende rendere la misura permanente con la legge di bilancio di fine anno. A ogni modo nel 2027 sono in programma le elezioni politiche: trovare il modo di finanziare strutturalmente una misura così onerosa diventerà quindi un problema del prossimo governo, anche se dovesse essere guidato ancora da Meloni, e non è detto che si decida di mantenerla. Anche perché la situazione che ha innescato il provvedimento, cioè la crisi energetica dovuta alla guerra in Medio Oriente, potrebbe cambiare.

La misura è stata annunciata un po’ a sorpresa. Nei giorni scorsi era emerso che il governo stava lavorando in effetti a un provvedimento sul bollo, ma si pensava al massimo a uno sconto e non a una completa esenzione. Ed è un annuncio sorprendente anche perché è un’esenzione che costerà miliardi di euro allo Stato, in un momento in cui il governo sta facendo fatica a racimolare qualche centinaio di milioni per continuare a prorogare di settimana in settimana lo sconto sulle accise, cioè le imposte di importo fisso su ogni litro di carburante.

La decisione di sospendere la riscossione del bollo è stata presa proprio all’interno del piano per contrastare il rincaro di benzina e gasolio innescato dalla guerra in Medio Oriente.

Da tempo il governo discuteva su come smettere di finanziare lo sconto sulle accise , che ha una forte valenza politica ma che rispetto a quanto costa ha effetti molto marginali sul costo dei carburanti, oltre a essere iniquo e talvolta controproducente.

La sospensione del bollo è una misura altrettanto popolare, e anche in questo caso con qualche effetto distorsivo: l’importo del bollo varia a seconda della potenza del veicolo, dunque l’esenzione ha un valore più alto per chi ha macchine più potenti, mentre è più contenuta per chi ne ha una più piccola. A questo si aggiunge che non ci sono soglie di reddito, dunque ne sarà beneficiato anche chi ha un reddito alto ma una macchina di piccola o media potenza.

Nei giorni scorsi era emerso che un eventuale intervento sul bollo avrebbe sostituito lo sconto sulle accise sul gasolio in vigore fino a giovedì 17 settembre, di cui il Consiglio dei ministri doveva decidere l’eventuale proroga. Ha comunque deciso di rifinanziare lo sconto, ma solo in parte: da circa 17 centesimi di euro al litro (IVA compresa) diventa di 12,2 centesimi dal 18 al 25 settembre, e poi si riduce ancora a 6 centesimi dal 25 settembre al 5 ottobre.

Dopo il 5 ottobre rientrerà in vigore il sistema delle cosiddette accise mobili, che destina i proventi aggiuntivi dell’IVA dovuti ai rincari a ridurre le accise.

items.title: Il bollo auto sarà abolito per auto di piccola e media potenza e motocicli. Una sola agevolazione per cittadino
items.summary: Lo ha deciso il Consiglio dei Ministri, anche se mancano ancora i dettagli tecnici riguardo alla potenza massima ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Il Consiglio dei Ministri ha deciso che per molte persone verrà abolito il bollo auto, almeno sulle auto di piccola e media potenza e i motocicli e almeno per il 2027. La potenza massima è stata identificata in 80 kW .

Secondo quanto riferito, riguarderà oltre il 70% delle auto in circolazione, ossia più di 13 milioni, presumibilmente gran parte - se non tutte - le utilitarie e le city car e oltre un milione di motocicli.

Un ulteriore dettaglio: ogni cittadino avrà diritto a una sola agevolazione . Insomma, viene abolito il bollo su un'auto o un motociclo, ma su eventuali altre mezzi di proprietà compatibili bisognerà pagarlo. Chi ha un'auto e uno scooter, per fare un esempio, pagherà il bollo su uno dei due veicoli, quello con potenza più alta. Inoltre, l'intervento non è legato all'ISEE.

Durante la conferenza stampa immediatamente successiva al Consiglio dei Ministri, la presidente del Consiglio, Giorgia Meloni, l'ha paragonata all'abolizione dell'IMU sulla prima casa e ha sottolineato che è stata pensata come rimedio strutturale contro il caro carburante. Lo sconto sulle accise sul gasolio proseguirà ancora per alcune settimane e a ottobre torneranno in vigore le accise mobili.

Poiché il bollo auto è una tassa regionale, il Governo compenserà direttamente le Regioni del gettito mancante.

Si tratta di un misura che più volte è stata proposta negli anni, essendo molto popolare, ma che non è mai stata implementata per via del costo miliardario sulle casse dello Stato.

items.title: Panasonic lancia una nuova ottica 20 mm Lumix full frame ultracompatta e leggera
items.summary: La nuova ottica per fotocamere full frame L-Mount offre un’apertura di F2.5, resistenza a schizzi e polvere e un corpo estremamente compatto e leggero pensato per abbinarsi alla full frame compatta Lumix S9 ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Panasonic ha annunciato oggi l’ultimo ingresso nel suo parco di ottiche Lumix per le fotocamere della gamma full frame con attacco L-Mount, la nuova LUMIX S 20 mm F2.5 (S-S20E-K). Come suggerisce il nome si tratta di un ultragrandangolo da 20 millimetri con apertura F2.5.

Il dato più significativo è però quello del design estremamente compatto, con una lunghezza di 40,9 mm e un peso di appena 142 grammi . Si tratta di un’ottica pensata in primo luogo per full frame compatte come la Lumix S9, ma che potrà trovare impiego in tutte quelle situazioni in cui serve contenere al minimo ingombro e peso.

È sostanzialmente lo stesso form factor dell’ottica LUMIX S 40 mm F2 lanciata lo scorso aprile che, secondo la stessa Panasonic, ha riscosso notevole interesse, tanto che è stato annunciato anche un nuovo kit di Lumix S9 proprio con la LUMIX S 40mm F2.

Panasonic spiega che la qualità dell’ottica è garantita dall’integrazione di tre elementi ottici asferici, mentre a livello di praticità si segnalano il tasto funzione Fn personalizzabile (la Lumix S9 per altro riceve un aggiornamento firmware proprio per aumentare la scelta delle funzioni assegnabili al tasto), il rivestimento al fluoro resistente a schizzi, polvere e gelo, le ghiera di messa fuoco anch’essa personalizzabile. La distanza minima di messa a fuoco è di 18 cm.

La nuova ottica sarà disponibile da ottobre in due colorazioni, nera e argento, ad un prezzo suggerito al pubblico di 499,99 euro.
